chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who has with him only the provision for his day: Should he give preference to the one who has the provision for his day over the one who has nothing, and should he give preference to the one who has the provision for a month over the one who has less than it, and the year in a similar manner, or is all of that the sufficiency (kafaf) for which he is not blamed?

So he (peace be upon him) said: It is a matter wherein the best of you is the one most eager for preferring (others) over himself, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'And they give preference over themselves, even though poverty may afflict them.'
And the other matter is that he is not blamed for sufficiency (kafaf), and the higher hand is better than the lower hand, and begin with those whom you support.

key_terms.الْأَثَرَةِ: Preference / Giving preference to others over oneself
key_terms.الْكَفَافُ: Sufficiency / The level of provision that exempts one from blame

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between sufficiency (kafaf) and preferring others (ithar) in Islamic charity and family support?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the legal baseline of 'kafaf' (sufficiency), where one is not blamed for providing only enough for oneself and dependents, and the spiritual excellence of 'ithar' (preferring others), which is a voluntary act of virtue. He cites the Quranic principle of the Ansar to illustrate that true superiority lies in self-sacrifice even in scarcity, while affirming that the 'upper hand' (giver) is superior to the 'lower hand' (receiver). This hadith establishes a nuanced hierarchy in Shia ethics, encouraging believers to transcend mere obligation and emulate the generosity of the Prophet's companions.
